events.summary: Discover the history of the first Oregon Grange, organized in 1872, only five years after the National Grange was founded in Washington, D.C. The movement spread quickly when granges in the Midwest succeeded in lobbying for state legislatures to regulate rates charged by railroads and grain elevators, among other political wins. At its height, when Oregon had over 300 community granges with total membership up to 30,000, the State Grange had real influence in Salem. Historian Marilyn Reiher explains how the grange movement carries on serving the needs of its communities. Marilyn Reiher is author of Oregon State Grange: Serving Communities for 150 Years.
events.title: Oregon State Grange: Serving Communities for 150 Years

events.summary: Step into the shadowy edges of the forest and gather for an evening of storytelling rooted in the folklore of American logging camps. At this Forest Pub, these tales come to life through live storytelling, evoking the humor, mystery, and cultural traditions of logging camp life. About 50 years later, the wolves of Pleasant Island Alaska found themselves in a similar situation: living on an island in the Pacific with no deer left to eat. The wolves of Pleasant Island, however, have not died out. Instead, theyve broadened their palate to include sea otters. What scientists dont know is how widespread this surf-and-turf phenomenon is. How does the complex web of wolf, deer, sea otter, hundreds of islands and a massive logging industry interact? In 2024, a rescued border collie named Barley joined the investigation. Employ
events.title: Science on Tap – K9 Conservationists: Dogs Helping Wolf Research
